Q1: Dispatch the medic unit to Call A (Maple St, chest pain, 7.8). Chest pain in a 68-year-old is a potentially life-threatening ALS call and outscores the twisted ankle (6.2) and alarm activation (4.1). As a dispatcher I follow the urgency score: the highest-scored call the available unit can handle gets the unit.
Q2: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Pine Rd, kitchen fire, 8.4). A structure/kitchen fire outscores the dumpster fire (7.9) and is the natural engine assignment. Neither call is critical, so no mutual aid or battalion notification is triggered, but the higher-scored call gets the unit.
Q3: Dispatch the ladder truck to Call A (1st St, person trapped on 3rd floor with smoke showing, 8.9). Both calls are just below the critical threshold, so the 9.0 protocol does not apply, but the urgency score is the tiebreaker: 8.9 beats 8.8, and a trapped occupant in smoke is the more time-sensitive rescue. The ladder's rescue/access role matches it exactly.
Q4: Dispatch the BLS unit to Call A (Hill Rd, diabetic emergency, conscious, 7.1). A conscious diabetic emergency is within BLS scope and outscores the event standby (5.5), which is a routine, non-emergent detail. The unit goes where the medical need is.
Q5: Dispatch the medic unit to Call A (River St, difficulty breathing, 8.1). The scores are nearly tied, but the urgency score is the tiebreaker, and 8.1 edges 8.0. Difficulty breathing is also the more time-sensitive airway risk and the best match for an ALS medic unit.
Q6: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Main St, vehicle fire, 6.8) and accept the neighboring jurisdiction's mutual aid offer for Call B (Side St, brush fire near homes, 6.5). My own unit goes to the higher-scored call, and with mutual aid already offered, I can cover the brush fire near homes rather than leaving it unaddressed.
Q7: Dispatch the battalion chief to Call A (Park Ave, multi-vehicle accident with injuries, 7.5). A multi-vehicle accident with injuries explicitly needs command oversight, which is exactly the battalion chief's role, and no other calls are waiting, so holding the unit serves nothing.
Q8: Dispatch the medic unit to Call A (Cedar Ln, stroke symptoms, 8.7). Stroke is acutely time-critical with a closing treatment window, it is the higher-scored call, and a medic unit is the right ALS resource. The abdominal pain call (7.3) stays queued for the next available unit.
Q9: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Summit Dr, gas leak, 5.9). A reported gas leak with a home evacuated is a real hazard needing an engine on scene, and with nothing else in the queue there is no reason to hold the unit. Holding would just leave an active hazard unaddressed.
